market_context: United States and general English-speaking market
title: Fresh vs. canned sardines: nutrition differences

seo.title: Fresh vs. canned sardines: protein, calcium and fat
seo.meta_description: Fresh and canned sardines are both protein-rich oily fish, but oil, sodium and edible bones change the nutrition. See a practical comparison.
seo.search_intent: Compare fresh and canned sardine nutrition

excerpt: Fresh sardines and canned sardines remain similar high-protein oily fish, but canning changes water content and often adds oil or salt. A raw sardine reference is around 185 calories and 21 g protein/100 g; Atlantic sardines canned in oil with edible bones provide about 208 calories, 24.6 g protein, 11.5 g fat and 382 mg calcium/100 g.
content_html:
Canning does not erase the nutritional identity of sardines, but it changes water content, packing medium, sodium and whether you eat the bones.

Protein remains high

A raw sardine reference is roughly 185 calories, 21 g protein and 10–11 g fat per 100 g. Atlantic sardines canned in oil, drained with bones, provide about 208 calories, 24.6 g protein and 11.5 g fat.

The canned fish is somewhat more concentrated after cooking and moisture loss.

Oil can raise calories

Oil-packed sardines retain some packing oil after draining. Water-packed or tomato-sauce products can have a different calorie and fatty-acid profile.

Edible bones are the standout difference

The canned-with-bones reference contains 382 mg calcium/100 g. Pressure processing softens the small bones enough to eat. A fresh fillet with the skeleton removed does not provide that same calcium concentration.

Sodium varies by can

Canned products usually contain added salt, but brands vary widely. A low-sodium or no-salt-added product can be very different from a heavily brined one.

Both still provide omega-3

Fresh and canned sardines contain EPA and DHA, vitamin B12 and vitamin D. If the can uses vegetable oil, some of the measured total fat comes from that packing oil rather than the fish itself.

Fresh sardines give you more control over seasoning; canned sardines add convenience and, when bones are eaten, a major calcium advantage.

faq.question: Do canned sardines have less protein?
faq.answer: No. The canned reference here provides 24.6 g/100 g, slightly more by weight than a raw reference because it is more concentrated.

faq.question: Why are canned sardines high in calcium?
faq.answer: The softened edible bones remain in the can and contain much of the fish's skeletal calcium.

faq.question: Are canned sardines higher in calories?
faq.answer: Oil-packed versions can be. The example is 208 calories/100 g versus roughly 185 for a raw sardine reference.

faq.question: Are canned sardines high in sodium?
faq.answer: They can be, but sodium varies greatly by brand and packing liquid.
